tooltip_popover.title: 1.1 Perfect Squares and Square Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Square and A Cube

children.name: Definition and Geometric Representation of Perfect Squares

tooltip_popover.title: Definition and Geometric Representation of Perfect Squares
tooltip_popover.content: A perfect square is formed by multiplying a natural number by itself: n * n = n^2. The area of a square with side length x units is x^2 square units. Perfect squares always possess an odd count of total factors.
tooltip_popover.example: Queen Ratnamanjuri's Will Puzzle: Lockers remain open if and only if their locker numbers are perfect squares because they have an odd number of factors.

children.name: Ending Digits and Odd Sum Patterns of Squares

tooltip_popover.title: Ending Digits and Odd Sum Patterns of Squares
tooltip_popover.content: The unit digits of all perfect squares can only be 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 9. Numbers ending in 2, 3, 7, or 8 can never be perfect squares. The sum of the first n consecutive odd natural numbers starting from 1 is equal to n^2.

tooltip_popover.title: 1.2 Cubic Numbers and Cube Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Square and A Cube

children.name: Definition and Volume Scale of Perfect Cubes

tooltip_popover.title: Definition and Volume Scale of Perfect Cubes
tooltip_popover.content: A cubic number or perfect cube is obtained by multiplying a natural number by itself three times: n * n * n = n^3. A 3D cube of side 1 cm forms larger unit-cube assemblies of side 2 cm (8 cubes), side 3 cm (27 cubes), etc.
tooltip_popover.example: Unit Cubes Assembly: 3x3x3 block composed of 27 unit cubes.

children.name: Prime Factorisation Method for Square Roots and Cube Roots

tooltip_popover.title: Prime Factorisation Method for Square Roots and Cube Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Square roots require grouping prime factors into pairs of identical primes. Cube roots require grouping prime factors into triplets of identical primes. To convert a non-cube into a perfect cube, multiply or divide by missing factor powers.
tooltip_popover.example: Activity ACT-1.1: Finding cube root of 27000 via prime factorisation -> 27000 = (2*2*2)*(3*3*3)*(5*5*5) -> Cube Root = 2*3*5 = 30.
